newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends weaker in U.S., market rocked by yen talk.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends weaker in U.S., market rocked by yen talk.

text.p: The dollar ended weaker after briefly tumbling to its lowest level in nearly four months against the yen as foreign exchange markets were roiled by rumors that the U.S. Treasury would support a stronger Japanese currency, experts said.
Specifically, market gossip claimed that a newsletter from a Washington-based consulting firm stated that Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin is calling for an exchange rate of 115 yen per dollar.
Yet subscribers to the newsletter contacted by Reuters denied having received such a report.

The talk, which hit currency markets late in the day, triggered previously set orders to sell dollars for yen. The already ailing dollar sank briefly to 116.95 yen, its lowest level since mid January.
Cynthia Cooley, a foreign exchange analyst and trader at United Gulf Bank of Bahrain in Boston, said "That must have been what caused the precipitous drop."
Stephen Jury, chief dealer at Union Bank of Switzerland, said: "The dollar was going down anyway. So when this story came out, that only exacerbated the situation."
The dollar closed at 117.30/40 yen and 1.6945/55 marks, down from 118.65/70 yen and 1.7055/65 marks at the open.
A surprising drop in a key gauge of inflation reported on Wednesday also weighed on the dollar as the data cast further doubt on prospects for a Federal Reserve interest rate hike next week.
The Labor Department reported the Producer Price Index (PPI) fell 0.6 percent in April, the largest decline since August 1993. With volatile food and energy items excluded, the PPI slid 0.1 percent.
Economists polled by Reuters had expected the PPI to be unchanged in April, with the core up 0.1 percent.

The Producer Price Index "added to the bearishness because as long as the perception is that the Fed is not tightening -- and I don't think it's priced in the market right now -- then you're going to see pressure on the dollar," said Edith Wolf, head of corporate sales at Credit Commerciale de France in New York.
Fed policymakers will meet next Tuesday to decide whether to tighten credit again. On March 25, they had increased the federal funds target rate to 5.50 percent from 5.25 percent.
Initially, the dollar had climbed against the mark in Europe after German central bank officials expressed approval of the current exchange rate level between the two currencies.
Speaking to reporters at an Austrian central bank conference in Vienna, Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke said a dollar exchange rate of around 1.70 marks was supported by economic data.

Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher also told reporters on Wednesday at a banking conference in Warsaw that present relations between the dollar and the mark were good, but he declined to specify an exact rate.
The dollar had climbed briefly to 1.7085 marks in Europe.

By the time that Bundesbank vice-president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum said the central bank was not especially concerned about the dollar's exchange rate, the currency had already retreated to trade slightly below 1.70 marks in New York.
Elsewhere, the dollar fell to 1.4355/65 Swiss francs from 1.4461/68, but rose to Canadian $1.3893/98 from C$1.3876/81. Sterling climbed to $1.6460/70 from $1.6370/75.
The Australian dollar slid to $0.7762/67 from $0.7790/00.
